properties.Name: The Hippodrome
properties.WhyShort: When Second Street was considered the Harlem of the South the Hippodrome theater was a key stop for many Black performers.
properties.WhyLong: The theater was then sold to Abe Lichtman theater chain in 1937. Specifically between the 1920s and the 1950s, the theater went through its own Harlem Renaissance where performers like Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, Ray Charles, Bill Robinson, and many other notable figures performed. In 1945, the theater caught fire but it was renovated and reopened in 1947 where it primarily focused on being a movie theater for the next decade but by the 1960s, the theater started closing down and opening up countless times where it served as a church for a little while but it no longer shined like it used to.

properties.Name: Hotel Eggleston
properties.WhyShort: Accommodated Black travelers to Jackson Ward. High profile individuals often stayed here.
properties.WhyLong: In 1942, Neverett A. Eggleston Sr. purchased Hotel Eggleston. Having amenities like a grill, dining room, and pool room the hotel became a staple. During World War 2, the hotel was a bustling business that catered to both locals and visiting celebrities such as Billie Holiday and Joe Louis. Hotel Eggleston became part of the fabric of Jackson Ward serving as a gathering place for the civil rights community, performers, and Black travelers. The hotel was a notable stop for Black travelers as it boasted modern amenities such as 24 hour food service and air conditioned rooms. Due to integration in the 1970s, the hotel’s success started to dwindle as people started to move away for new opportunities. By the 1980s the hotel was vacant.

properties.Name: Consolidated Bank and Trust
properties.WhyShort: Oldest continuously operated Black owned bank in the United States.
properties.WhyLong: In 1929, St Luke Penny Saving Bank and Second Street Savings Bank merged to create the Consolidated Bank and Trust. The bank opened on January 2 1930, operating out of St Luke Penny Saving Bank’s old building. A year later, the bank merged with Commercial Bank and Trust. Through the Depression, the bank continued to thrive until the twenty-first century. In 2005 Abigail Adams National Bank purchased Consolidated Bank and Trust which ended the bank’s distinction as the oldest Black operated bank in the United States.

properties.Name: Rayo Theater
properties.WhyShort: A theater that showed a wide array of performances and kept people coming back with their weekly theme nights.
properties.WhyLong: The Rayo theater opened in the summer of 1921. The theater underwent lots of owner changes until 1924 when Charles L. Somma leased the venue. That year the theater saw a revitalization following the management of Mr. Droste who turned the struggling venue into a vibrant hub for entertainment. The theater became renowned for its diverse offerings of performances such as vaudeville acts, plays, and motion pictures. Due to its exceptional customer services the theater developed a devoted customer base. Rayo became well known for its unique weekly giveaways such as a crate of live chickens to envelopes of money.

properties.Name: IBPOEW Club/Elks Home Capital City Lodge
properties.WhyShort: A fraternal organization for colored/black people; helped raised money for scholarships.
properties.WhyLong: In the Old Mansion of W.L. Taylor, the Improved Benevolent Practice Order of Elks (IBPOEW) housed their lodge in 1930. This organization was founded on the basis of having a fraternal society for people of color. The IBPOEW really supported the advancement of African Americans with the society raising $700,000 for scholarships towards African Americans to attend college.This happened under Finley Wilson who was appointed the Grand Exalted Ruler in 1922. He helped the organization grow in terms of membership and new lodges. They also largely supported civil rights, raised war bonds, and helped African Americans get jobs and also be able to unionize.
properties.Image1Cite: "Capital City Lodge of Elks Enters New Second St. Home." Richmond Planet, October 4, 1930.

properties.Name: Slaughter's Hotel
properties.WhyShort: Also known for its very good meals, accommodating to Black travelers, and had many famous people stay.
properties.WhyLong: Slaughter’s Hotel was first opened by Richard Slaughter around 1924. By 1931 the hotel moved to a larger location across the street. Slaughter’s was well known for its dedication to high quality food and accommodations for Black travelers at a time when options were limited. From the 1930s-1940s the hotel was a prominent establishment that attracted lots of notable guests such as Oliver Hill. Gertrude Taylor took over hotel management in 1945 after Richard Slaughter passed away. Under Taylor’s management the hotel thrived as a gathering place for organizations such as the NAACP and the Richmond Crusade of Voters. Along with this, the hotel also served as a meeting place for political, social, and community leaders. Through the 1970s the hotel continued to be a staple with its club sandwich becoming a local legend. In the early 1990s the hotel was demolished to make way for the Jackson Center.
